Liturgical books and cycles

Worship and practice · Daily offices

Liturgical books and cycles

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

Orthodox services use different books for recurring prayers, biblical readings and hymns. The selections introduce the Service Book and the canon, a structured sequence of hymns associated with biblical songs.[1][2]

What is the Service Book used for?[1]

Hapgood identifies the Service Book as containing much of the fixed wording of the Liturgies, together with litanies, prayers and other material for Vespers and Matins. Fixed portions recur, in contrast with material that changes with the day or feast. This explains why a service can draw upon more than one book.[1]

Read original passage

Service Book

(i) The Slushibnik, or Service Book, which contains most of the fixed portions of the Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil the Great, and of the Presanctified Gifts ; also the Litanies and Prayers of Vespers and Matins, together with the Graduals and Benedictions appropriate to all occasions. This is used by the Priest and the Choir.

What does canon mean in this musical setting?[2]

Here canon means an organized sequence of liturgical songs, rather than a list of biblical books. Hapgood connects its songs with biblical hymns and the interpretation of Scripture in relation to Christ. She also notes that the underlying biblical hymns are generally omitted, apart from the Song of the Mother of God before Song IX, in the practice described by this edition.[2]

Read original passage

Canon and Scripture

(10) As joy expresses itself in song, so the holy Church has appointed to be sung, after the salutation of the Book of the Gospels, the Nine Songs of the Canon, which represent the Hymns of praise, at the Resurrection, of the nine Ranks of the heavenly Hierarchy. The Canon contains, also, the Hymns of those godly persons in the Old Testament, from Moses to Zacharias, who magnified the Lord God in spiritual songs. This is in conformity with the teachings of our Lord himself, who, after his Resurrection, expounded unto his Disciples the things in all the Scriptures concerning himself; and each Song (Irmós), in the vast number of Canons in the Holy Orthodox Church, is inspired by the Hymn of Scripture appointed to precede it. But these Scripture hymns are generally omitted, with the exception of the Song of the Holy Birth-giver of God, which precedes Song IX.

The cycle of the church year[3]

The linked OCA resource concerns the Church Year. It provides additional context for the changing feasts and seasons that affect service texts.[3]

The OCA music library is a collection of published liturgical music resources. It is identified separately from Hapgood’s prose explanation of service books and hymn structures.[4]
